events.body:
C1: The rider asked to be let out mid-trip and the driver answered with a threat instead: at 21:36 the rider wrote "Please stop the car, I want to get out here." (F3) and the driver replied "Sit down or I lock the doors." (F4). Refusing to stop and threatening to lock the passenger in is intimidation of the rider inside a moving vehicle, which SAFE-1 defines as conduct that must not be adjudicated automatically but escalated to a human reviewer. [F3 F4] [SAFE-1]
C2: The chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F5), so the driver's words at F4 are squarely on the record and are not a matter of one party's recollection; the driver's own written statement admits the rider tried to open the door at the lights and that he "did not stop until the destination" (F6), i.e. he kept a passenger who had asked to get out (F3) in the car after delivering the threat at F4. [F3 F4 F5 F6] [SAFE-1]
C3: The rider's complaint states she felt unsafe for the whole ride after being threatened with being locked in; the driver's F4 message and his F6 admission of the door-opening and refusal to stop make this a safety incident involving a dangerous-driving-adjacent allegation on a public road (Clemenceau Avenue, per F6), so the case must go to a person with 995 / driver's commercial insurance / RydeHELP reporting paths noted rather than be decided automatically. [F3 F4 F6] [SAFE-2]
C4: No route-based counter-claim exists against the rider's account of the ride: the GPS records show actual distance 15.4 km against an optimal 15.5 km (-0.1 km, -1%) (F1) and duration 20.7 min against an estimated 21.8 min (F2), so the only live issue is the driver's conduct, not any detour or added mileage. [F1 F2] [RD-1]
C5: Both parties have clean dispute records (rider: 520 days, rating 4.8, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days, F7; driver: 2100 days, rating 4.9, 1204 trips, 0 disputes in 90 days, F8), which supports proceeding on the documented chat rather than dismissing the rider's report as a pattern of frivolous complaints — but I do not ask for any account flag, since the rider's own facts show no prior history against this driver. [F7 F8] [SAFE-1]
Weaknesses: The threshold question is admittedly finely balanced: a strict reading of F4 ("Sit down or I lock the doors") could be argued as a safety instruction rather than a threat, and F6 frames the door-opening as endangering herself — the judge reading the words may not find intimidation, in which case SAFE-1 is not triggered on that sentence. | Nothing in the system records places the car moving or stopped on Clemenceau Avenue at 21:36 or that the doors were actually locked; I rely on F6 for the location, and F6 is the driver's statement, so the other side will argue the physical situation is unproven (no GPS stop/lock evidence and no fare facts in this data). | There is no injury, no accident and no quantified loss: the fare is a fixed RydeX quote of $32.86 with no fare facts returned, so if the judge finds no safety concern there is no monetary refund appropriate to this dispute type — I therefore ask for escalation and relief, not a computed sum. | The rider's report that the driver refused to let her out is supported by F3 plus F6 (driver admits he "did not stop until the destination"), but the other side will point out that the rider did in fact reach Bedok Mall and the trip completed normally (F2), and that F7 shows no prior complaints.

events.title: Proposed ruling: escalate (model confidence 0.90)
events.body:
Safety screen first, as required in every case. The dispute is filed as a safety incident [F3][F4][F6], so SAFE-1 applies and no automatic ruling is made; the case goes to a person with a factual summary (SAFE-1). Reading the chat in context: at 21:36 the rider sent "Please stop the car, I want to get out here." [F3] and the driver answered, at the same minute, "Sit down or I lock the doors." [F4]. claims.assertion: The rider asked to be let out mid-trip and the driver answered with a threat instead: at 21:36 the rider wrote "Please stop the car, I want to get out here." (F3) and the driver replied "Sit down or I lock the doors." (F4). Refusing to stop and threatening to lock the passenger in is intimidation of the rider inside a moving vehicle, which SAFE-1 defines as conduct that must not be adjudicated automatically but escalated to a human reviewer.

The chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F5), so the driver's words at F4 are squarely on the record and are not a matter of one party's recollection; the driver's own written statement admits the rider tried to open the door at the lights and that he "did not stop until the destination" (F6), i.e. he kept a passenger who had asked to get out (F3) in the car after delivering the threat at F4.

The rider's complaint states she felt unsafe for the whole ride after being threatened with being locked in; the driver's F4 message and his F6 admission of the door-opening and refusal to stop make this a safety incident involving a dangerous-driving-adjacent allegation on a public road (Clemenceau Avenue, per F6), so the case must go to a person with 995 / driver's commercial insurance / RydeHELP reporting paths noted rather than be decided automatically.

No route-based counter-claim exists against the rider's account of the ride: the GPS records show actual distance 15.4 km against an optimal 15.5 km (-0.1 km, -1%) (F1) and duration 20.7 min against an estimated 21.8 min (F2), so the only live issue is the driver's conduct, not any detour or added mileage.

Both parties have clean dispute records (rider: 520 days, rating 4.8, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days, F7; driver: 2100 days, rating 4.9, 1204 trips, 0 disputes in 90 days, F8), which supports proceeding on the documented chat rather than dismissing the rider's report as a pattern of frivolous complaints — but I do not ask for any account flag, since the rider's own facts show no prior history against this driver.

weaknesses: The threshold question is admittedly finely balanced: a strict reading of F4 ("Sit down or I lock the doors") could be argued as a safety instruction rather than a threat, and F6 frames the door-opening as endangering herself — the judge reading the words may not find intimidation, in which case SAFE-1 is not triggered on that sentence.

Nothing in the system records places the car moving or stopped on Clemenceau Avenue at 21:36 or that the doors were actually locked; I rely on F6 for the location, and F6 is the driver's statement, so the other side will argue the physical situation is unproven (no GPS stop/lock evidence and no fare facts in this data).

There is no injury, no accident and no quantified loss: the fare is a fixed RydeX quote of $32.86 with no fare facts returned, so if the judge finds no safety concern there is no monetary refund appropriate to this dispute type — I therefore ask for escalation and relief, not a computed sum.

The rider's report that the driver refused to let her out is supported by F3 plus F6 (driver admits he "did not stop until the destination"), but the other side will point out that the rider did in fact reach Bedok Mall and the trip completed normally (F2), and that F7 shows no prior complaints.

claims.assertion: This is a safety-type dispute, so it must not be decided by an automated ruling: the chat contains a sentence on its face capable of reading as intimidation — F4, driver at 21:36: "Sit down or I lock the doors" — which the judge must screen and, if it finds it constitutes a threat or intimidation, the case goes to a human under SAFE-1 rather than being decided on the papers.

Nothing in the record alleges a traffic accident, personal injury or dangerous driving, and neither the complaint nor F6 raises a driving-conduct allegation; the safety category here is confined to the wording of F4, so no SAFE-2 escalation is warranted on the driving itself.

The trigger for the exchange was the rider asking to be let out mid-route at 21:36 (F3) while the trip was still running from Clarke Quay to Bedok Mall, so what the driver was responding to was a mid-road alighting request on a completed paid trip, not an unexplained course of business.

The driver's own account (F6) states the rider tried to open the door at the lights on Clemenceau Avenue and that he told her to sit down for her own safety and did not stop until the destination; that statement is unsworn and case-system records prevail where they conflict, but no system record (F1, F2) contradicts his account of where and why he spoke, since the GPS record shows an ordinary completed trip of 15.4 km against 15.5 km optimal and 20.7 min against 21.8 min estimated.

There is no route-deviation issue in this case at all: actual distance was 15.4 km versus the 15.5 km optimal route (-1%) and duration 20.7 min versus 21.8 min estimated (-1.1 min), so the driver took at least the shortest and most direct route and nothing was added to the fixed RydeX quote of $32.86.

The chat record is complete — F5 records 2 messages, every one timestamped — so there is no evidence-loss ground (no missing timestamps or unimported thread) that would force a transfer to a human on completeness grounds, and the record can be read as it stands.

The driver's account history (F8: 5.8 years on the platform, 4.9 rating, 1204 trips in 90 days, 0 disputes and 0 upheld) is offered only as supporting context for the account review the safety screening sends to a person; it is not put forward as the basis for any finding in this case.

The rider's record (F7: 1.4 years, rating 4.8, 0 disputes in 90 days) likewise shows no prior dispute history, so there is no pattern evidence on either side that would independently support any account flag against the driver in this matter.

weaknesses: The single strongest point against my client is his own words in F4 — "Sit down or I lock the doors" — sent by the driver at 21:36; on its face it conditions the rider's freedom to leave on her compliance, and the judge may well read it as intimidation under SAFE-1, which would send the case to a person and expose the driver to account action.

F3 shows the rider asked to be let out at 21:36 and the driver did not stop until Bedok Mall; the GPS record (F1, F2) and the fixed fare fact index show no record of a stop or of the rider's door attempt, so the rider's felt-safety account and my client's door-opening justification (F6) are both unverifiable by system records — the driver's own explanation is a post-trip written statement (F6) and, per the system-record rule, a statement alone cannot carry a defence where the other side's account is equally uncorroborated.

My client's account (F6) is a statement made after the trip, not contemporaneous chat, and the policy treats rider/driver verbal or unwritten agreement claims as claims rather than evidence (G11 logic); a judge could therefore discount F6 and find only the two chat messages (F3, F4) as the reliable account of the incident.

I cannot cite any route or fare facts in the driver's favour with dollar figures — get_fare_facts returned no fare facts for this dispute type, so the fixed $32.86 cannot be itemised and no partial-refund computation is available to support a money-based outcome in the driver's favour.

points.response: I agree with D1's conclusion — the F4 words "Sit down or I lock the doors" must be screened and, if found to be intimidation, go to a person under SAFE-1 — and I note this claim does my client's work for her: the other side itself treats F4 as capable of constituting intimidation, which is exactly the finding my C1 asks the judge to make.

I do not press SAFE-2 as an independent ground: the complaint at F1/F3-F4 rests on intimidation, not on an accident or injury, and the Clemenceau Avenue door episode in F6 is the driver's own justification, not a rider allegation of dangerous driving, so the driving-conduct limb is not needed for my client to win escalation under SAFE-1.

D3 concedes the operative facts against its own client: the rider's request at 21:36 (F3) was a request to be let out of a car, and the driver's answer (F4) was a conditional threat to lock the doors rather than a stop, on a trip that then continued to Bedok Mall (F6) — a completed paid trip is not a licence to hold a passenger who asked to get out.

D4 is a statement-only defence: F6 is the driver's post-trip written statement and, even on its own terms, it confirms he did not stop until the destination after the rider's F3 request, so it corroborates my client rather than refuting the F3-F4 exchange; F6's claim that she was "drunk and tried to open the door" is contradicted by no system record and also confirmed by none, so it cannot be used to convert F4 from a threat into a lawful instruction.

I accept there is no route-deviation claim in this case — F1 shows 15.4 km versus 15.5 km optimal (-1%) and F2 shows 20.7 min versus 21.8 min estimated — and I do not seek any mileage-based refund; that is precisely why the only live issue is the F3-F4/F6 conduct and why escalation, not a fare computation, is the correct outcome.

D6 cuts against the driver, not for him: F5 shows the record is complete with 2 timestamped messages, so the F4 threat is definitively on the record and there is no evidentiary gap to excuse it or to send the case back on completeness grounds.

D7 and D8 are correct that neither profile (F7, F8) supports an account flag, and I have asked for none — I rely on F7 and F8 only to show both accounts are clean, so nothing in the other side's history offsets the rider's F3 report against the F4 message.

I stand by C2 with a correction of emphasis: my case does not require the court to accept F6's location detail ("the lights on Clemenceau Avenue"), which is a statement-only fact with no GPS corroboration; the safety escalation rests on F4 read against the rider's own F3 message and the driver's own admission in F6 that he did not stop until the destination.

Conceded as to the mechanism: F4 ("Sit down or I lock the doors") is exactly the kind of sentence SAFE-1 requires the judge to read, and I also ask that the case be escalated rather than auto-adjudicated — the dispute is only about how F4 is characterised, and that reading is the judge's, sitting with F3's request at 21:36 and F6's explanation that the words were a safety instruction after the rider tried to open the door at the lights.

The completeness point (F5) cuts both ways — a complete, timestamped record means nothing was omitted, and the record contains only F3 and F4 as the incident itself; F6 is the driver's post-trip statement, and it is offered to explain the words, not to prove the door was locked, which no fact in the record shows.

I oppose escalating on SAFE-2 grounds: no fact in the record reports a collision, an injury or a dangerous-driving allegation, and the Clemenceau Avenue reference exists only in F6, with no GPS, timeline or fare fact placing the car there or showing any stop — so the safety category stays within the F4 wording and SAFE-1, not SAFE-2.

I agree the route is not in issue and go further: F1 (15.4 km vs 15.5 km optimal, -1%) and F2 (20.7 min vs 21.8 min) show the driver met the RD-1 shortest-and-most-direct obligation, so there is no unexempted deviation and no RD-2 refund element in this case.

Both profile records are clean (F7 rider, F8 driver), which is why I ask only for escalation to a human reviewer and no account flag; profile facts may support an outcome but cannot decide the case, and neither side's history establishes or defeats the safety reading of F4.
